fixes.explanation: Right, baker. The verse says, "…the farmers will plant and enjoy the fruit." (Jeremiah 31:5) The ones who plant are the ones who enjoy it. That's a promise worth a little dance.

I see where you went, friend, but it's not the word here. God says, "For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn." (Jeremiah 31:9) "Master" sounds like a boss, and the verse picks a family word instead. "Firstborn" is a family word, so Father fits.

The farmers did show up earlier in this passage, friend, but this verse picks a different picture. It says, "The One who scattered Israel will gather them and keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock." (Jeremiah 31:10) The picture is a shepherd and his flock. Sheep, not soil.

Yes, baker. God says, "Their life will be like a well-watered garden, and never again will they languish." (Jeremiah 31:12) To languish is to droop and wither. A garden with plenty of water is the picture He picks for their life back home.

Right, baker. Ephraim says, "I was ashamed and humiliated because I bore the disgrace of my youth." (Jeremiah 31:19) He owns it out loud, which is not an easy thing to do. I think that takes real guts.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "Return, O Virgin Israel, return to these cities of yours." (Jeremiah 31:21) Those are her own cities. Right before that comes the instruction, "Set up the road markers, put up the signposts."

Moving sounds reasonable, friend, but that's not the promise. God says, "Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel." (Jeremiah 31:4) Nothing in the verse talks about moving her. And look at that word "Again." God is promising to build her up once more.

That's it, baker. "Again you will take up your tambourines and go out in joyful dancing." (Jeremiah 31:4) The tambourines are coming out for a party. That's a lot of jingling, and every bit of it is joyful.

Hiding is a fair guess for a watchman's call, friend. But the watchmen say, "Arise, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God!" (Jeremiah 31:6) That's a call to go UP, not to hide in. The direction is toward Zion.

Being tested sounds like a pop quiz, friend, and nobody signs up for those. The LORD tells them to say, "O LORD, save Your people, the remnant of Israel!" (Jeremiah 31:7) That's a request for rescue. It comes right after He says to make their praises heard.

"Judge" is a serious word, friend, but it's not the one here. The LORD says to ask, "O LORD, save Your people, the remnant of Israel!" (Jeremiah 31:7) The prayer asks Him to save. And it comes wrapped in praise, since He first says to make their praises heard.

Not quite, friend. God says He will gather them "…including the blind and the lame, expectant mothers and women in labor." (Jeremiah 31:8) That list names the blind, the lame and expectant mothers, so it isn't only the strong and healthy. He also says they will return as a great assembly.

That's right, baker. God says, "For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn." (Jeremiah 31:9) Father and firstborn are family words. So God speaks about Ephraim the way a dad speaks about his firstborn.

"Maker" is a good word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. He says, "For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn." (Jeremiah 31:9) "Firstborn" is a family word, so it goes with Father.

That's it, baker. "The One who scattered Israel will gather them and keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock." (Jeremiah 31:10) The same One who scattered is the One who gathers. And He keeps them the way a shepherd keeps his flock.

Yes, baker. God says, "I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow." (Jeremiah 31:13) The mourning gets turned into joy. And for their sorrow, He gives comfort and joy.

Wisdom is a fine thing, friend, but it's not in this verse. God says, "I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow." (Jeremiah 31:13) Joy shows up twice in that one verse. Wisdom isn't on the list.
Yes, baker. Ephraim says, "Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God." (Jeremiah 31:18) He asks to be restored so he can return. And the reason he gives is that the LORD is his God.

Payback is a natural thing to want, friend, but Ephraim doesn't ask for it. He says, "Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God." (Jeremiah 31:18) The only thing he asks for is to be restored. His request has nothing in it about anyone else.

Being left is a fear a lot of us carry, friend, but it's not what God says here. He says, "Though I often speak against him, I still remember him." (Jeremiah 31:20) The word is "remember." He goes on to say His heart yearns for him.
Not here, friend. God says, "Though I often speak against him, I still remember him." (Jeremiah 31:20) The word in the verse is "remember." Then He says His heart yearns for Ephraim.

Staying put is cozy, friend, but that's not the call. The verse says, "Return, O Virgin Israel, return to these cities of yours." (Jeremiah 31:21) Right before it, the instruction is to set up road markers and put up signposts. I think that sounds like a road for travelers, not for people staying put.

That's the word, baker. The LORD asks, "How long will you wander, O faithless daughter?" (Jeremiah 31:22) Just before that, He says, "Set up the road markers, put up the signposts." (Jeremiah 31:21) Then comes the question about wandering.

Hiding is a fair guess, friend, but the question isn't about that. The LORD asks, "How long will you wander, O faithless daughter?" (Jeremiah 31:22) Wandering means moving around with nowhere settled. That's the question He puts to her.

Boasting isn't the question, friend. The LORD asks, "How long will you wander, O faithless daughter?" (Jeremiah 31:22) The verse is about wandering. Just before it, the call is to set up road markers and put up signposts.

After so much weeping in this passage, I can see why that came to mind, friend. But when God restores them, they say, "May the LORD bless you, O righteous dwelling place, O holy mountain." (Jeremiah 31:23) That's a blessing, not a lament. A blessing is what He says they will speak.

That's right, baker. God says, "…I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak." (Jeremiah 31:25) If you've ever dragged yourself to the end of a long week, you know what weary feels like. That's the kind of soul He says He will refresh.

"Proud" is a different word, friend. God says, "…I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak." (Jeremiah 31:25) The soul He names is the weary one. Weary means worn out, tired to the bone.

"Wicked" isn't the word, friend. God says, "…I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak." (Jeremiah 31:25) The verse names the weary soul and all who are weak. Those are the ones He says He will refresh and replenish.

You've got it, baker. The one speaking says, "At this I awoke and looked around. My sleep had been most pleasant to me." (Jeremiah 31:26) The sleep is called most pleasant, not troubled. The passage closes on that note.
